# PRD: Header Dark Mode Toggle

**Author:** Relay Studio Agent
**Date:** 2026-05-09
**Status:** Draft

---

## 1. Problem Statement

Users spend significant time inside the app, often across different lighting conditions — bright offices in the morning, dim rooms at night, or high-glare outdoor environments. The app currently offers only a single, fixed light theme. This forces users to endure eye strain in low-light environments, makes the app feel visually harsh late in the day, and leaves users whose operating systems are already set to dark mode feeling like the app is out of sync with the rest of their digital environment. There is no escape hatch: users cannot adapt the interface to their context without leaving the app entirely.

---

## 2. Solution

A dark mode toggle appears persistently in the app header. Users can click or tap it at any time to switch between a light theme and a dark theme. The chosen theme applies instantly, without a page reload, and is remembered the next time the user opens the app. Users who have configured their operating system to prefer dark mode will find the app already matches their preference on first visit. Authenticated users will find their preference follows them across devices and browsers.

---

## 3. User Stories

- **US-001:** As a general user, I want a clearly visible toggle in the app header, so that I can switch between light and dark themes without hunting through settings menus.
- **US-002:** As a general user, I want the theme to switch instantly when I activate the toggle, so that I do not have to wait for a page reload or experience a flash of unstyled content.
- **US-003:** As a general user, I want my chosen theme to be remembered when I close and reopen the browser tab, so that I do not have to re-set my preference every session.
- **US-004:** As a new user visiting the app for the first time, I want the app to automatically respect my operating system's dark/light mode preference, so that my first experience already feels comfortable without any manual setup.
- **US-005:** As an authenticated user, I want my theme preference to follow me when I log in on a different device or browser, so that my experience is consistent everywhere I use the app.
- **US-006:** As a user with motion sensitivity, I want any theme-transition animation to be suppressed when I have "reduce motion" enabled in my OS, so that I do not experience discomfort during the toggle.
- **US-007:** As a screen reader user, I want the toggle to have a clear, descriptive accessible label that updates to reflect the current state (e.g. "Switch to dark mode" / "Switch to light mode"), so that I always know what action the control will perform.
- **US-008:** As a keyboard-only user, I want to be able to reach and activate the dark mode toggle using the Tab and Enter/Space keys, so that I can change the theme without a mouse.

---

## 4. Implementation Decisions

### 4.1 Data Contract

**Entity: `ThemePreference`**

This is a lightweight preference record, not a full user profile entity. It exists in two scopes:

| Layer | Mechanism | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Anonymous / unauthenticated | Browser `localStorage` entry keyed `theme_preference` | Falls back to system preference if absent |
| Authenticated | `UserPreference` record in the database, field `theme` | Loaded at session start; overrides localStorage on login |

**Fields on the persisted `UserPreference` record (extending any existing preferences model):**

| Field | Type | Nullable | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `theme` | `enum('light', 'dark', 'system')` | No | `'system'` | `'system'` means defer to OS `prefers-color-scheme` |
| `updated_at` | `timestamp` | No | `now()` | Updated on every toggle |

**Lifecycle / visibility state:**
- `'system'` is the implicit default for all users who have never explicitly toggled — it is the "unset" state and should be treated as valid, not as missing data.
- The active theme applied to the UI is derived at runtime: if `theme === 'system'`, read the OS media query; otherwise apply the stored value directly.
- There is no "deleted" or "archived" notion for this preference — the record is upserted on every change.

**Relationships:**
- `UserPreference.theme` is a field on the existing user preferences model (or a new `UserPreference` record with a `user_id` foreign key to the `User` entity, if no preferences model exists yet). Follow the project's existing one-to-one relationship convention between `User` and preferences.

---

### 4.2 Tracer Bullet Slices

> **Slice 1 — In-session theme switching**
> *Behavior:* A user clicks the toggle in the header; the entire app immediately re-renders under the dark (or light) color scheme for the duration of the browser session, with no page reload.
> *Cuts through:* Theme context/store holding the active theme value; CSS custom properties or Tailwind `dark:` class applied at the root `<html>` or `<body>` element; header toggle component reading and writing to the theme store; design-token layer defining all dark-mode color overrides.

> **Slice 2 — Preference persisted to localStorage**
> *Behavior:* A user toggles the theme, closes the tab, reopens the app, and finds the same theme already applied — no flash of the wrong theme on load.
> *Cuts through:* Theme store reading from `localStorage` on initialization before first paint; write-through to `localStorage` on every toggle; SSR/hydration guard if the app is server-rendered (theme class applied server-side or deferred gracefully to avoid hydration mismatch).

> **Slice 3 — System preference detection on first visit**
> *Behavior:* A brand-new user who has never toggled arrives with their OS set to dark mode; the app loads already in dark mode without any action on their part.
> *Cuts through:* Theme store initialization logic reading `window.matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)')` when no stored preference exists; a `MediaQueryList` listener that updates the active theme in real time if the OS setting changes mid-session while `theme === 'system'`.

> **Slice 4 — Authenticated user preference synced to backend**
> *Behavior:* A logged-in user toggles the theme; logs out; logs back in on a different device; the correct theme is applied immediately after authentication without any manual re-toggling.
> *Cuts through:* `UserPreference.theme` field upserted in the database on each toggle via an authenticated API endpoint; theme preference loaded as part of the user session payload at login and hydrated into the theme store before first paint; conflict resolution rule: server preference wins over any stale localStorage value on login.

> **Slice 5 — Accessible and keyboard-operable toggle**
> *Behavior:* A keyboard-only user tabs to the toggle in the header, sees a visible focus ring, presses Space or Enter, and the theme changes — the toggle's accessible label updates to reflect the new action available.
> *Cuts through:* Toggle component rendered as a native `<button>` (not a `<div>`); `aria-label` computed from current theme state; focus-visible styles applied in both light and dark tokens; `prefers-reduced-motion` media query suppressing the CSS transition on theme switch.

---

### 4.3 Other Implementation Decisions

**Theme store (the central module):**
The theme store is the single source of truth for the active theme. It is responsible for: reading the initial value (server preference → localStorage → OS media query → default `'system'`); writing through to localStorage on every change; exposing a `resolvedTheme` computed value (`'light'` or `'dark'`, never `'system'`) that consumers use to render. Components and API routes must not read localStorage or media queries directly — they go through the store.

**CSS theming strategy:**
All color values must be expressed as design tokens (CSS custom properties). The dark theme is activated by toggling a `data-theme="dark"` attribute (or equivalent class) on the root element — not by duplicating stylesheets. This ensures a single toggle point and prevents a flash of the wrong theme if the attribute is set synchronously before paint.

**API endpoint for authenticated preference:**
A dedicated preference-update endpoint (e.g. a PATCH on the user preferences resource) handles theme writes. It must be authenticated, idempotent, and return the updated preference record. The client should optimistically update the store without waiting for the response, then reconcile on error.

**Flash of incorrect theme (FOIT) prevention:**
If the app uses server-side rendering, the theme must be applied before the page is sent to the client (via a cookie that mirrors the localStorage value, readable server-side) or via a blocking inline script that reads localStorage and sets the root attribute synchronously before the React tree hydrates. The chosen approach must be documented in the architecture decision log.

**Conflict resolution on login:**
When a user logs in, the server-side `UserPreference.theme` value replaces any value currently in localStorage. If the server value is `'system'` (never explicitly set), the existing localStorage value is preserved and written back to the server as the authoritative preference.

**Error handling:**
- If the preference API call fails, the toggle still works locally (optimistic update is kept); a non-blocking error is logged; no user-facing error message is shown for this low-stakes preference.
- If localStorage is unavailable (private browsing, storage quota), the theme store degrades gracefully to in-memory-only state with no error surfaced to the user.

---

## 5. Testing Decisions

**What makes a good test here:** tests should assert observable behavior — "the root element has `data-theme='dark'` after clicking the toggle" — not implementation details like "the store's internal `_theme` variable changed." Tests should not mock the theme store when testing components that consume it; use a real (or thin wrapper) store instance instead.

**Unit tests (Vitest or Jest, matching project convention):**
- **Theme store logic:** cover all initialization paths: stored `'dark'` in localStorage → resolves to `'dark'`; stored `'system'` + OS dark → resolves to `'dark'`; stored `'system'` + OS light → resolves to `'light'`; nothing stored, OS dark → resolves to `'dark'`; nothing stored, OS light → resolves to `'light'`. Cover the write-through: toggling from light to dark writes `'dark'` to localStorage.
- **`resolvedTheme` computation:** all six combinations of the `theme` enum value and OS media query result.

**Component tests (Testing Library, matching project convention):**
- **Toggle component:** renders with correct initial `aria-label`; clicking changes the label; clicking applies the correct `data-theme` attribute to the root element; focus ring is visible (snapshot or class assertion); Space and Enter keys activate the toggle.
- **Reduced motion:** when `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` is active (mocked via `matchMedia`), the CSS transition class is absent.

**Integration tests:**
- **Login hydration:** simulate a login response that includes `theme: 'dark'`; assert the theme store and root element reflect `'dark'` after hydration, overriding a stale `'light'` in localStorage.
- **Preference persistence round-trip:** toggle theme → reload (re-initialize store from localStorage) → assert same theme is active.

**E2E tests (Playwright or Cypress, matching project convention):**
- Toggle from light to dark, reload page, assert dark theme is active.
- Log in as a user whose server-side preference is `'dark'`; assert the page loads in dark mode without a flash.
- Keyboard navigation: Tab to toggle, press Space, assert theme changes.

**Acceptance criteria:** all slices in §4.2 must have at least one passing integration or E2E test before the feature is considered shippable.

---

## 6. Out of Scope

| Item | Reason deferred |
|---|---|
| Per-page or per-component theme overrides | Adds significant complexity to the token system; the toggle is a global preference. |
| A "sepia" or "high-contrast" third theme | Valid accessibility enhancement but a separate feature with its own design-token work. |
| Scheduled / automatic theme switching by time of day | Useful but requires a scheduling mechanism; not part of the core toggle feature. |
| Admin controls to force a default theme for all users in an org | Enterprise-only feature; the toggle is user-scoped. |
| Theme selection from a settings page | The header toggle covers the primary use case; a settings-page entry point can be added later when a full preferences UI is built. |
| Exporting or importing theme preferences | Not a user-reported need at this time. |
| Dark-mode-specific image assets or illustrations | Design team deliverable tracked separately; the toggle ships with color-token-level dark mode only. |

---

## 7. Further Notes

- **Design token audit required before Slice 1 ships:** all color usages in the existing UI must be expressed via CSS custom properties or the equivalent token layer before the dark theme can be activated globally. Any hard-coded color values (hex literals, raw Tailwind color classes) will need to be migrated. This is a prerequisite task, not part of the slice itself, and may surface significant scope.
- **Cookie strategy for SSR flash prevention:** the choice between a server-readable cookie and a synchronous inline script has hydration and caching implications. This decision should be made jointly with the infrastructure team and recorded in the ADR before Slice 2 begins.
- **System preference listener lifecycle:** the `MediaQueryList` listener added in Slice 3 must be properly removed when the theme store is torn down to avoid memory leaks in single-page navigation contexts.
- **Open question — icon or label?** The toggle's visual treatment (sun/moon icon, a labelled switch, or a text button) is a design decision not resolved in this PRD. The accessibility requirements in US-007 and US-008 apply regardless of visual form.
- **Related work:** this feature is a prerequisite for any future "branded themes" or "white-label theme customization" work, as it establishes the token-based theming architecture those features would extend.
- **Analytics consideration (future):** tracking toggle frequency could inform whether `'system'` should become the permanent default for new users or whether explicit light/dark is preferred — deferred to post-launch.

# PRD: Dashboard PDF Export

**Author:** Relay Studio Agent
**Date:** 2026-05-09
**Status:** Draft — Needs Triage

---

## 1. Problem Statement

Dashboard users frequently need to share insights with people who don't have access to the application — executives, clients, external partners, or colleagues in other tools. Today, there is no reliable way to do this. Users resort to taking browser screenshots (which are cropped, low-resolution, and miss off-screen content), using the browser's built-in print function (which produces poorly paginated, unstyled output that breaks chart layouts), or manually recreating charts in slide decks.

This is especially painful for analysts and managers who produce regular reports. Every export is a manual, time-consuming workaround that produces a result that doesn't look professional and doesn't faithfully represent what they were looking at — it captures the page, not the dashboard state.

Users need a way to turn what they see on screen into a clean, shareable artifact without leaving the application or losing fidelity.

---

## 2. Solution

A clearly labeled **Export as PDF** action, available directly on the dashboard, that captures the current view — including all applied filters, active date ranges, and visible panels — and downloads a formatted, print-ready PDF to the user's device.

The exported document will look like the dashboard: charts render correctly, tables don't overflow, and the layout is consistent regardless of screen size. It will include a header with the dashboard name, the export timestamp, and a summary of any active filters, so recipients always have context without needing to ask the sender.

During export, users will see clear in-progress feedback and receive a meaningful error message if something goes wrong, rather than a silent failure.

---

## 3. User Stories

- **US-001:** As a dashboard viewer, I want to trigger a PDF export of the current dashboard, so that I can download a shareable snapshot without leaving the application.
- **US-002:** As a data analyst, I want the exported PDF to reflect my currently active filters and date range, so that the document accurately represents the analysis I was performing.
- **US-003:** As a manager, I want all visible charts and metric tiles to appear in the PDF at full fidelity, so that I can include the export in presentation decks and stakeholder reports without reformatting.
- **US-004:** As a dashboard viewer, I want the exported PDF to include the dashboard name and the timestamp of the export, so that recipients know what they are looking at and when the data was captured.
- **US-005:** As a dashboard viewer, I want to see a loading indicator while the PDF is being generated, so that I know the export is in progress and haven't accidentally triggered it multiple times.
- **US-006:** As a dashboard viewer, I want to receive a clear error message if the PDF export fails, so that I know something went wrong and can try again rather than waiting indefinitely.
- **US-007:** As a dashboard admin, I want to control whether PDF export is enabled on a given dashboard, so that sensitive or embargoed dashboards cannot be exported and distributed without authorization.
- **US-008:** As a dashboard viewer, I want the exported PDF filename to default to the dashboard name and export date, so that downloaded files are easy to identify in my filesystem without renaming them manually.

---

## 4. Implementation Decisions

### 4.1 Data Contract

**New or Extended Entities:**

**`DashboardExportConfig`** — a settings record that controls export behavior per dashboard. Extends (or associates with) the existing `Dashboard` model.

| Field | Type | Nullable | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | UUID | No | generated | Primary key |
| `dashboardId` | UUID (FK) | No | — | References the `Dashboard` entity |
| `exportEnabled` | boolean | No | `true` | Whether PDF export is permitted |
| `createdAt` | timestamp | No | now() | — |
| `updatedAt` | timestamp | No | now() | — |

- **Lifecycle / visibility:** `exportEnabled: false` gates the export action entirely — the UI suppresses the button, and the server endpoint returns a `403` if called directly. Only dashboards with `exportEnabled: true` are eligible for export. There is no "draft" or "soft-delete" state on this config; it is a live toggle.
- **Relationship:** One `DashboardExportConfig` per `Dashboard` (1:1). Created lazily on first admin configuration; if no record exists, the system defaults to `exportEnabled: true`.

**`ExportRequest`** — a short-lived job record representing an in-flight or recently completed PDF export. Used to support async generation and to prevent duplicate submissions.

| Field | Type | Nullable | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | UUID | No | generated | Primary key |
| `dashboardId` | UUID (FK) | No | — | The source dashboard |
| `requestedBy` | UUID (FK) | No | — | References the `User` entity |
| `status` | enum | No | `pending` | `pending \| processing \| completed \| failed` |
| `snapshotState` | JSONB | No | — | Serialized filter set, date range, and panel visibility at export time |
| `fileUrl` | string | Yes | `null` | Populated once the PDF is stored and ready |
| `errorMessage` | string | Yes | `null` | Populated on `failed` status |
| `createdAt` | timestamp | No | now() | — |
| `completedAt` | timestamp | Yes | `null` | Populated when `status` reaches terminal state |

- **Lifecycle / visibility:** Only records with `status: 'completed'` have a valid `fileUrl`. The UI only surfaces the download link when status is `completed`. Records with `status: 'failed'` surface the `errorMessage`. Records in `pending` or `processing` state drive the loading indicator. Stale `ExportRequest` records (older than 24 hours) are cleaned up by a background job and are never shown to the user.
- **Relationship:** Many `ExportRequest` records per `Dashboard`; many per `User`.

---

### 4.2 Tracer Bullet Slices

> **Slice 1 — Basic end-to-end export**
> *Behavior:* The user clicks "Export as PDF" on a dashboard, the server generates a PDF of the current layout using the default view state, and the browser downloads it with a filename of `[DashboardName]_[YYYY-MM-DD].pdf`.
> *Cuts through:* `ExportRequest` creation (status: pending → processing → completed), server-side headless render of the dashboard layout, file storage and signed URL generation, UI export button triggering the request, polling for completion, and triggering browser download on `fileUrl` arrival.

> **Slice 2 — State-aware export (filters + date range)**
> *Behavior:* The user applies filters and a custom date range, then exports; the resulting PDF reflects exactly those selections — charts render with filtered data, and a filter summary header appears at the top of the first page.
> *Cuts through:* Serialization of active UI state into `snapshotState` JSONB on the `ExportRequest`, server-side renderer consuming `snapshotState` to reconstruct the dashboard context, filter summary rendering in the PDF header template.

> **Slice 3 — In-progress feedback and error recovery**
> *Behavior:* While export is generating, the button is replaced by a spinner with "Generating PDF…" text; if generation fails, the spinner is replaced by an inline error message with a retry action.
> *Cuts through:* `ExportRequest` status polling on the client, UI state machine mapping `pending/processing → loading`, `failed → error with retry`, `completed → download trigger`; `errorMessage` surfacing from the `ExportRequest` record.

> **Slice 4 — PDF metadata header**
> *Behavior:* Every exported PDF includes a styled header on each page showing the dashboard name, export timestamp (in the user's timezone), and a compact list of active filters, so recipients have full context without asking the sender.
> *Cuts through:* PDF header template component in the render service consuming `dashboardName`, `exportedAt`, and the filter summary extracted from `snapshotState`; user timezone resolved from the `User` record and passed into the render context.

> **Slice 5 — Admin export access control**
> *Behavior:* A dashboard admin toggles "Disable PDF Export" in dashboard settings; the export button immediately disappears for all viewers of that dashboard, and direct API calls return a `403`.
> *Cuts through:* `DashboardExportConfig.exportEnabled` toggle in the admin settings UI, server-side gate on the export endpoint checking `exportEnabled` before creating an `ExportRequest`, client-side conditional rendering of the export button based on the config value fetched with the dashboard.

---

### 4.3 Other Implementation Decisions

**Render service boundary:** PDF generation is handled by a dedicated export render service (headless browser-based), not inline in the main API server. The main API creates the `ExportRequest` record, hands off the job to the render service (via message queue or background job system following existing patterns), and polls/updates status. This keeps the main request path non-blocking and isolates the heavy rendering dependency.

**Snapshot state contract:** The `snapshotState` JSONB field on `ExportRequest` must capture the full filter predicate, date range (start/end as ISO strings), and a list of visible panel IDs. The render service must be able to reconstruct the dashboard's data query from this object alone — it does not read live UI state.

**File storage:** Completed PDFs are stored in the application's existing object storage layer (same bucket/provider used for other file uploads). The `fileUrl` is a short-lived signed URL (TTL: 15 minutes) generated at the time the client fetches the completed `ExportRequest`. It is not a permanent public URL.

**Polling vs. WebSocket:** The client polls the `ExportRequest` status endpoint on a 2-second interval, capped at 90 seconds total. If the job has not reached a terminal state by 90 seconds, the client surfaces a timeout error and the `ExportRequest` is marked `failed` by the server. This avoids introducing a WebSocket dependency for a low-frequency operation.

**Duplicate prevention:** If a user clicks "Export" while an `ExportRequest` for their user+dashboard combination is already in `pending` or `processing` state, the server returns the existing in-flight record rather than creating a duplicate. The UI disables the button during this window.

**Filename generation:** The PDF filename follows the pattern `[DashboardName]_[YYYY-MM-DD].pdf` where the date is the export date in the user's local timezone. Non-filesystem-safe characters in the dashboard name are replaced with underscores.

**Error handling:** Render failures (chart data fetch timeout, headless browser crash) set `status: 'failed'` and populate `errorMessage` with a user-readable string. The server never exposes internal stack traces in `errorMessage`.

**`DashboardExportConfig` default:** If no `DashboardExportConfig` record exists for a dashboard, the system treats `exportEnabled` as `true`. The config record is only written when an admin explicitly changes the setting.

---

## 5. Testing Decisions

**What makes a good test here:** Tests should verify observable behavior — what the user or API consumer sees — not internal wiring. Tests should not assert on private render-service internals; they should assert on the shape of the `ExportRequest` lifecycle, the correctness of `snapshotState` serialization, and the PDF content at a structural level (headers present, filter summary populated, correct page count).

**Unit tests (Vitest or project-standard framework):**
- `snapshotState` serializer: covers empty filter set, multi-filter combinations, missing date range (defaults), and a panel visibility list with mixed show/hide states.
- `DashboardExportConfig` defaulting logic: asserts that a missing config record is treated as `exportEnabled: true`, and that a record with `exportEnabled: false` produces a `403` gate.
- Filename generation utility: covers dashboard names with special characters, names exceeding filesystem limits, and timezone edge cases at midnight UTC.

**Integration tests (project-standard API test layer, real DB):**
- `POST /export-requests`: asserts that a new `ExportRequest` is created in `pending` state with correctly serialized `snapshotState`; asserts that a duplicate request for an in-flight job returns the existing record.
- `GET /export-requests/:id`: asserts status transitions (`pending → processing → completed`), `fileUrl` presence on `completed`, and `errorMessage` presence on `failed`.
- Export gate: asserts that dashboards with `exportEnabled: false` return `403` from the export endpoint regardless of user role.

**E2E tests (Playwright or project-standard browser test layer):**
- Happy path: user applies a filter, clicks "Export as PDF", sees the loading state, and receives a downloaded file with the correct filename pattern.
- Error path: server returns a `failed` status; user sees the inline error message and the retry button is actionable.
- Access control: admin disables export on a dashboard; a viewer session on that dashboard does not render the export button.

**Acceptance criteria requiring test coverage:**
- All unit tests for `snapshotState` serialization pass before the server-side render service is integrated.
- E2E happy-path test must pass in CI against a real render service instance (not mocked) before the feature is considered shippable.

---

## 6. Out of Scope

- **Scheduled / recurring PDF exports:** Automatically emailing a PDF on a schedule (e.g., every Monday morning) is a separate feature that requires notification infrastructure. Not included here.
- **Custom PDF branding/theming:** Allowing users to inject a custom logo, color scheme, or font into the PDF is a post-launch enhancement. The initial export uses the application's default visual style.
- **Exporting a subset of panels:** Letting users pick which panels to include (e.g., "export only this chart") is deferred. The initial feature exports the full visible dashboard layout.
- **Sharing via link (no download):** Generating a shareable URL that others can open to view the PDF in-browser is out of scope. Export always results in a download.
- **Export to other formats (CSV, XLSX, PNG):** Only PDF is in scope for this feature. Other export formats are separate features with different data contracts and UI surfaces.
- **Mobile-optimized PDF layout:** The PDF is generated from the desktop dashboard layout. Mobile-specific responsive layout considerations for the rendered output are deferred.
- **Audit log of exports:** Recording who exported what and when for compliance purposes is deferred. The `ExportRequest` table incidentally captures this data, but a formal audit log UI and retention policy are out of scope.
- **Role-based export permissions (beyond admin toggle):** Fine-grained permission control (e.g., "only Editor role can export") is deferred. The initial implementation is binary: export is either enabled or disabled for the whole dashboard.

---

## 7. Further Notes

- **Render service choice:** The headless rendering approach (e.g., Puppeteer/Playwright-based service) is recommended over client-side libraries (html2canvas + jsPDF) because it guarantees visual fidelity, handles complex SVG charts correctly, and doesn't depend on the client's screen resolution or browser quirks. This is especially important for dashboards with data-dense tables or custom chart components.
- **PDF page layout:** The render service should target A4 landscape by default, as most dashboards are wider than they are tall. This should be a configuration-level default, not a user-facing option in this iteration.
- **Timezone handling:** The user's timezone must be resolved at request time and passed explicitly to the render service. Relying on the server's system timezone will produce incorrect date range labels in the PDF header.
- **Open question — large dashboards:** Dashboards with many panels or very large datasets may take longer than the 90-second polling cap to render. A performance budget for the render service (target: <30s for dashboards with up to 20 panels) should be defined before implementation begins, and the render service should be load-tested against realistic dashboard sizes.
- **Related feature:** This PRD is a prerequisite for any future "Scheduled Reports" feature, which would reuse the `ExportRequest` + render service pipeline triggered by a cron rather than a user action.
- **`ExportRequest` record cleanup:** A background cleanup job (outside this PRD's implementation scope) should purge `ExportRequest` records and their associated stored files after 24 hours. Retention policy should be confirmed with legal/compliance before the feature ships if the application operates in a regulated industry.

# PRD: Keyboard Navigation Shortcuts

**Author:** Relay Studio Agent
**Date:** 2026-05-09
**Status:** Draft

---

## 1. Problem Statement

Power users on the platform spend a disproportionate amount of time moving their hand between keyboard and mouse just to navigate lists and trigger search. In a team productivity tool — where users cycle through tasks, tickets, or feed items dozens of times per day — this constant context-switch interrupts flow and slows down the very work the platform is meant to accelerate.

Today, every navigation action requires a click: clicking an item to select it, clicking into the search bar to start filtering. For users who prefer to stay on the keyboard — engineers triaging issues, PMs scanning backlogs, analysts reviewing feeds — there is no alternative. The absence of keyboard shortcuts signals that the product is not built for power users, and it creates friction that compounds with every session.

---

## 2. Solution

Users gain a set of keyboard shortcuts that let them move through any list and reach the search bar without ever touching the mouse.

Pressing **`j`** advances the selection to the next item in the current list; pressing **`k`** moves it to the previous item. The selected item is visually highlighted and scrolled into view automatically. Pressing **`/`** instantly focuses the search input — the cursor lands there and the user can start typing their query immediately.

Shortcuts are active by default and are scoped so that they do not fire while the user is already typing in a text field, textarea, or rich-text editor. A discoverable help overlay (triggered by **`?`**) shows the full shortcut reference so new users can learn the bindings without consulting external docs.

The result: navigating an entire list and initiating a search becomes a seamless, keyboard-first experience — consistent with power-user expectations for productivity software.

---

## 3. User Stories

- **US-001:** As a power user, I want to press `j` to move to the next item in a list, so that I can advance through items without lifting my hand from the keyboard.
- **US-002:** As a power user, I want to press `k` to move to the previous item in a list, so that I can move backwards through items without using the mouse.
- **US-003:** As a power user, I want the currently selected item to be visually distinguished and automatically scrolled into view, so that I always know where I am in the list.
- **US-004:** As a user, I want to press `/` to instantly focus the search input, so that I can start filtering content without clicking into the search bar.
- **US-005:** As a user, I want keyboard shortcuts to be suppressed when I am typing in a text field or rich-text editor, so that normal typing is never accidentally intercepted.
- **US-006:** As a new user, I want to press `?` to see a shortcut reference overlay, so that I can discover available keyboard shortcuts without consulting external documentation.
- **US-007:** As a user, I want to press `Escape` to dismiss the shortcut overlay and deselect the active keyboard-navigation item, so that I can return to a neutral state at any time.
- **US-008:** As an accessibility-conscious user, I want keyboard-navigated item selection to update the appropriate ARIA attributes, so that screen readers correctly announce the focused item.

---

## 4. Implementation Decisions

### 4.1 Data Contract

Keyboard shortcuts in this initial version are **stateless from a persistence standpoint** — the bindings are fixed constants defined in a shared shortcut registry (a client-side module), not stored in the database. No new PostgreSQL entities are introduced.

The one extension to existing models is on the **User Preferences** entity (or equivalent user-settings record), which must gain:

| Field | Type | Nullable | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `keyboardShortcutsEnabled` | `boolean` | No | `true` |

- **Lifecycle/visibility:** A user with `keyboardShortcutsEnabled = false` receives no shortcut event handling. The setting is visible and editable from user preferences UI. The feature treats `true` as the active state.
- **Relationship:** One-to-one with the existing `User` model, stored in the user preferences table (or as a column on whatever user-settings record the project already uses).

The **shortcut registry** is a pure client-side data structure: a typed map of `ShortcutKey → ShortcutDefinition`, where `ShortcutDefinition` holds the display label, description, and handler identity. No database persistence.

### 4.2 Tracer Bullet Slices

> **Slice 1 — j/k item navigation on a single list**
> *Behavior:* A user opens any list view, presses `j` or `k`, and the next or previous item is highlighted and scrolled into view; pressing `Enter` on a highlighted item activates it identically to a mouse click.
> *Cuts through:* Shortcut registry (key bindings), global keyboard listener (mounted at app shell level), list component (accepts and renders a `selectedIndex` or equivalent focused-item state), ARIA `aria-selected` attribute updates.

> **Slice 2 — `/` focuses search**
> *Behavior:* A user presses `/` from anywhere on a list page; focus jumps to the search input, a cursor appears, and the user can type immediately — pressing `Escape` returns focus to the list.
> *Cuts through:* Shortcut registry, global keyboard listener, search input component (exposes a `focus()` ref handle), focus-trap/return logic.

> **Slice 3 — Shortcut suppression in text fields**
> *Behavior:* A user editing a text field or textarea presses `j`, `k`, or `/`; the characters appear in the field as normal and no navigation side-effect occurs.
> *Cuts through:* Global keyboard listener (adds `isInputFocused` guard checking `event.target` tag name and `contenteditable` attribute before dispatching any shortcut).

> **Slice 4 — `?` help overlay**
> *Behavior:* A user presses `?` from any list view; a modal overlay appears listing all registered shortcuts with their key and description; pressing `Escape` or clicking outside dismisses it.
> *Cuts through:* Shortcut registry (iterated to render entries), overlay/modal component, shortcut registration for the `?` key itself.

> **Slice 5 — User preference to disable shortcuts**
> *Behavior:* A user navigates to their preferences, toggles "Enable keyboard shortcuts" off, and from that point forward `j`, `k`, `/`, and `?` no longer trigger any navigation behavior.
> *Cuts through:* `keyboardShortcutsEnabled` field on user preferences (read via existing preferences API), global keyboard listener (checks preference before processing any key event), preferences UI (toggle control with label).

### 4.3 Other Implementation Decisions

**Shortcut registry as a deep module:** All shortcut definitions live in a single registry module. Components subscribe to shortcuts by registering handlers — they do not wire up raw `keydown` listeners themselves. This keeps the event model centralized and testable in isolation.

**Global keyboard listener:** Mounted once at the application shell level (not per-page or per-component). It reads the current route context and the user preference before dispatching. Shortcuts that are not relevant to the current view are no-ops, not unregistered — this avoids registration/teardown complexity.

**Scope-aware suppression:** The listener must check `event.target` for `INPUT`, `TEXTAREA`, `SELECT`, and any element with `contenteditable="true"` before firing any shortcut. This is a hard rule with no exceptions.

**ARIA compliance:** The list component receiving `j`/`k` navigation must set `role="listbox"` or `role="list"` with appropriate `aria-activedescendant` or `aria-selected` updates so screen reader users benefit from the same navigation.

**Scroll behavior:** When `j`/`k` changes the active item, the list must call `scrollIntoView({ block: 'nearest' })` on the newly active element. This prevents the selected item from going off-screen in long lists.

**`/` focus guard:** The `/` shortcut must call `event.preventDefault()` to suppress the browser's built-in quick-find feature before focusing the search input.

**No custom keybinding persistence in this version:** Users cannot remap keys. The bindings are fixed. Remapping is explicitly out of scope (see §6).

**Preference API:** The `keyboardShortcutsEnabled` setting is served via the existing user-preferences API endpoint using the project's standard server-side data-fetching pattern (Next.js server components or API route, whichever is established). No new endpoint is introduced if one already covers user preferences.

---

## 5. Testing Decisions

**What makes a good test here:** Test observable behavior (does the correct item become selected? does focus land on the search input?) not implementation details (was a specific internal function called?).

**Unit tests — Shortcut registry (Vitest):**
- Registering a shortcut returns it from the registry lookup.
- Registering a duplicate key overwrites the previous handler (or throws, per the chosen policy — must be explicit).
- Iterating the registry for the help overlay returns all registered entries in stable order.

**Unit tests — Input suppression logic (Vitest):**
- `isInputFocused` returns `true` for `INPUT`, `TEXTAREA`, `SELECT`, and `contenteditable` targets.
- `isInputFocused` returns `false` for `DIV`, `LI`, `BUTTON`, and `null`.

**Unit tests — List navigation state (Vitest or React Testing Library):**
- `j` on the first item in a five-item list selects index 1.
- `k` on the first item does not go below index 0 (boundary clamp).
- `j` on the last item does not exceed the list length (boundary clamp).
- `j`/`k` with `keyboardShortcutsEnabled = false` does not change selection.

**Integration tests — Search focus (React Testing Library + jsdom):**
- Pressing `/` calls `focus()` on the search input element.
- Pressing `Escape` after `/` returns focus to the previously focused element.

**Integration tests — Help overlay (React Testing Library):**
- Pressing `?` renders the overlay with all registered shortcut descriptions.
- Pressing `Escape` dismisses the overlay.

**E2E tests (Playwright):**
- Full navigation flow: open a list page → press `j` three times → confirm third item is visually highlighted and in viewport → press `Enter` → confirm the item's detail view loads.
- Search flow: press `/` → type a query → confirm search results update → press `Escape` → confirm focus returns.
- Typing in a text field: click into a text input → press `j` → confirm the character `j` appears in the input and no list navigation occurs.

**Acceptance criteria:** All Vitest unit and integration tests pass in CI. Playwright e2e tests pass against the staging environment. Axe accessibility audit on the list component with keyboard navigation active reports zero new violations.

---

## 6. Out of Scope

- **Custom / remappable keybindings:** Users cannot change which keys trigger which actions. Remapping requires a key-conflict resolution system and persistent storage of per-user bindings. Deferred as a follow-on.
- **Shortcut chording or multi-key sequences:** All shortcuts in this version are single keystrokes. Sequences like `g i` (go to inbox) are out of scope.
- **Mobile / touch support:** Keyboard shortcuts are inherently desktop-only. No equivalent gesture mappings are introduced here.
- **Per-list shortcut context switching:** All lists share the same `j`/`k` bindings. Contextual shortcuts (e.g., different behavior per page type) are not part of this version.
- **Vim-style additional bindings** (`gg` to jump to top, `G` to jump to bottom, `dd` to delete, etc.): Only `j`, `k`, `/`, `?`, and `Escape` are in scope.
- **Onboarding / tooltip coachmarks for shortcuts:** Discovery is handled only by the `?` overlay. Inline tooltip hints or onboarding flows are a separate UX feature.
- **Syncing shortcut preference across devices:** The `keyboardShortcutsEnabled` preference is stored per user (not per device), so it syncs naturally — but multi-device conflict resolution is not a concern in this feature's scope.

---

## 7. Further Notes

- **Inspiration / prior art:** Gmail (`j`/`k`/`/`) and Linear both popularized this exact shortcut set for productivity tools. Users migrating from those tools will find the bindings immediately familiar — this is intentional.
- **Open question:** Should `j`/`k` wrap around at list boundaries (i.e., pressing `j` on the last item jumps to the first), or clamp? The current spec says clamp. This is worth validating with user research before finalizing — wrapping can feel disorienting in long lists.
- **Open question:** What constitutes a "list" for the purposes of these shortcuts? If the page has multiple independent lists (e.g., a sidebar list and a main content list), which one does `j`/`k` target? A scoping heuristic (last-clicked list, or the list containing the currently focused element) must be decided before Slice 1 ships.
- **Accessibility note:** The `?` overlay must be keyboard-dismissible and trap focus internally while open. If the project has an existing accessible modal/dialog component, that should be reused rather than a new overlay implementation created.
- **Related feature:** A future "command palette" (⌘K) feature would supersede some of the discoverability role currently served by the `?` overlay. The shortcut registry designed here should be structured so the command palette can consume it as a data source without significant rework.
- **Analytics consideration:** It may be valuable to instrument shortcut usage (which keys are used, how often) to justify future investment in expanded bindings. No analytics instrumentation is in scope for this version, but the shortcut registry is a natural chokepoint to add it later.

# PRD: In-App Notification Center

**Author:** Relay Studio Agent
**Date:** 2026-05-09
**Status:** Draft

---

## 1. Problem Statement

Team members using the platform today have no single place to learn what has happened in their workspace. When a colleague assigns them a task, leaves a comment, or changes a status, the only way to discover it is to manually navigate to that area of the app — if they remember to check at all. There is no persistent signal that something needs their attention, no history of past events, and no way to clear the noise once they've caught up. As a result, users miss time-sensitive updates, context is lost between sessions, and team communication suffers because action items go unacknowledged. The cognitive cost of staying up to date is pushed entirely onto the user.

---

## 2. Solution

A notification center, accessible from a persistent bell icon in the top navigation bar, gives users a real-time-adjacent view of everything that has happened across their workspace. A badge on the bell immediately signals how many unread items are waiting. Opening the panel reveals a chronological list of notifications, with unread items visually distinct from read ones. Users can mark a single notification as read, or clear their entire unread count with one click. When a notification is no longer relevant, they can dismiss it individually or bulk-dismiss everything for a clean slate. Clicking a notification navigates directly to the relevant item, collapsing the discovery gap that exists today.

---

## 3. User Stories

- **US-001:** As a team member, I want to see a badge on the navigation bell icon showing my unread notification count, so that I can know at a glance whether something needs my attention without leaving my current task.
- **US-002:** As a team member, I want to open a notification center panel from any page, so that I can review all recent workspace activity in one place regardless of where I am in the app.
- **US-003:** As a team member, I want unread notifications to be visually distinct from read ones, so that I can immediately identify which items I haven't seen yet.
- **US-004:** As a team member, I want to click a notification to navigate directly to the related resource, so that I can take action on the triggering event without searching for it manually.
- **US-005:** As a team member, I want to mark an individual notification as read, so that I can acknowledge it without removing it from my notification history.
- **US-006:** As a team member, I want to mark all notifications as read at once, so that I can clear my unread badge quickly after catching up on activity.
- **US-007:** As a team member, I want to dismiss an individual notification, so that I can remove items that are no longer relevant from my notification list.
- **US-008:** As a team member, I want to bulk-dismiss all notifications at once, so that I can fully clear my notification center with a single action when I no longer need the history.
- **US-009:** As a team member, I want to see an empty state in the notification panel when all notifications have been dismissed, so that I understand the center is intentionally clear and not broken.
- **US-010:** As a team member, I want the unread badge count to update immediately after I take any read or dismiss action, so that the count always reflects the true state of my notifications without a page refresh.

---

## 4. Implementation Decisions

### 4.1 Data Contract

**Entity: `Notification`**

| Field | Type | Nullable | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | `uuid` | No | `gen_random_uuid()` | Primary key |
| `userId` | `uuid` | No | — | FK → `User.id`, cascade delete |
| `type` | `enum NotificationType` | No | — | e.g. `task_assigned`, `comment_added`, `mention`, `status_changed` |
| `title` | `text` | No | — | Short human-readable summary |
| `body` | `text` | Yes | `null` | Optional longer description |
| `resourceType` | `text` | Yes | `null` | Entity kind the notification refers to (e.g. `'task'`, `'project'`) |
| `resourceId` | `uuid` | Yes | `null` | ID of the triggering entity; not a hard FK to preserve flexibility |
| `readAt` | `timestamptz` | Yes | `null` | `null` = unread; populated timestamp = read |
| `dismissedAt` | `timestamptz` | Yes | `null` | `null` = visible; populated timestamp = dismissed/hidden |
| `createdAt` | `timestamptz` | No | `now()` | |

**Lifecycle / Visibility State:**

- **Visible to the user** = `dismissedAt IS NULL`. All queries powering the notification center UI **must** gate on this condition.
- **Unread** = `dismissedAt IS NULL AND readAt IS NULL`. Drives the badge count and unread visual treatment.
- **Read** = `dismissedAt IS NULL AND readAt IS NOT NULL`. Visible in the panel but no longer highlighted.
- **Dismissed** = `dismissedAt IS NOT NULL`. Excluded from all user-facing queries; retained in the database for audit/analytics.

**Relationships:**
- `Notification.userId` → `User.id` (many-to-one). A `User` has many `Notification` records. Deleting a user cascades to their notifications.

**Recommended index:** `(userId, dismissedAt, createdAt DESC)` — supports the primary listing query as volume grows.

---

### 4.2 Tracer Bullet Slices

> **Slice 1 — Notification list with unread badge**
> *Behavior:* A logged-in user opens the notification center panel via the nav bell icon and sees their most recent non-dismissed notifications in descending order, with unread ones visually highlighted; the bell icon shows a badge equal to the unread count.
> *Cuts through:* `Notification` model + database migration; server-side listing query scoped to `userId` and gated on `dismissedAt IS NULL`, ordered by `createdAt DESC`, limit 50; unread count query for badge; notification center panel component; badge component wired into the top navigation bar; Next.js API route or server action serving both queries.

> **Slice 2 — Mark individual notification as read**
> *Behavior:* A user clicks "Mark as read" on a single unread notification; it immediately loses its unread visual treatment, and the badge count decrements by one.
> *Cuts through:* `PATCH /api/notifications/[id]/read` endpoint setting `readAt = now()` scoped to the current user; optimistic UI state update in the notification panel; badge count recomputed client-side; server returns 404 if the notification does not belong to the requesting user.

> **Slice 3 — Mark all notifications as read**
> *Behavior:* A user clicks "Mark all as read" in the panel header; every unread notification transitions to the read visual state and the badge drops to zero in a single interaction.
> *Cuts through:* `PATCH /api/notifications/read-all` endpoint issuing a single bulk `UPDATE` setting `readAt = now()` for all records matching `userId = current AND readAt IS NULL AND dismissedAt IS NULL`; full panel re-render reflecting read state; badge count reset to zero.

> **Slice 4 — Dismiss individual notification**
> *Behavior:* A user clicks the dismiss control on a single notification; it disappears from the panel immediately, and the badge count adjusts if the notification was unread.
> *Cuts through:* `PATCH /api/notifications/[id]/dismiss` endpoint setting `dismissedAt = now()` scoped to the current user; notification removed from the panel list via UI state update; badge recomputed; 404 guard on ownership.

> **Slice 5 — Bulk dismiss all notifications**
> *Behavior:* A user clicks "Dismiss all" in the panel; every notification disappears and the empty state is shown, with the badge dropping to zero.
> *Cuts through:* `PATCH /api/notifications/dismiss-all` endpoint issuing a single bulk `UPDATE` setting `dismissedAt = now()` for all records where `userId = current AND dismissedAt IS NULL`; panel list cleared; empty-state component rendered; badge zeroed.

> **Slice 6 — Navigate to resource from notification**
> *Behavior:* A user clicks the body of a notification that has a `resourceType` + `resourceId`; they are taken to the deep link for that resource, and the notification is marked as read in the same round-trip.
> *Cuts through:* Client-side click handler resolving `resourceType` + `resourceId` to an app route; `readAt` set via the same `PATCH /api/notifications/[id]/read` call before navigation; notification transitions to read state in the panel (panel may be closed by the navigation).

---

### 4.3 Other Implementation Decisions

**API surface:** All notification endpoints must authenticate via the existing session/auth middleware and scope every query and mutation to `req.user.id`. Cross-user access must return `403`, not `404`, to avoid leaking record existence.

**Badge cap:** The unread badge count displayed in the UI must cap at a configurable maximum (suggested: 99, rendered as "99+") to prevent layout overflow in the navigation bar.

**Initial load size:** The notification panel fetches the 50 most recent non-dismissed notifications on open. No pagination is implemented in this iteration (see §6).

**Notification creation (write side):** Out of scope for this PRD, but the `Notification` model and its `type` enum must be defined in a way that allows other parts of the codebase to insert records without modification to the notification center's read-side code. A lightweight server-side notification service module — accepting an event type, a `userId`, and optional `resourceType`/`resourceId` — should define the write contract so feature teams can integrate.

**Real-time delivery:** The panel fetches data on open. No WebSocket or SSE polling is included in this iteration (see §6).

**`NotificationType` enum extensibility:** The enum is defined in the database and in the TypeScript type layer; it must be designed for additive extension as new event types are introduced. Adding a new type must not require changes to the notification center's rendering logic — the panel renders `title` and `body` agnostically.

**Empty state:** When the fetched list is empty (all dismissed or no notifications exist), the panel renders a designated empty-state component rather than a blank area.

**Bulk operations performance:** Mark-all-read and dismiss-all must execute as a single `UPDATE … WHERE userId = $1` statement, never as per-record loops, to stay performant as notification volume grows.

**Optimistic UI:** All single-record and bulk actions update the client-side list state optimistically before the server response resolves, with a rollback on error, to keep the panel feeling instant.

---

## 5. Testing Decisions

**What a good test looks like:** Tests verify observable, user-facing behavior — what is returned by an API or rendered in the UI — not internal implementation details like which ORM method was called or how a module is structured internally.

**Unit tests (Vitest):**
- Notification query service: cover the `dismissedAt IS NULL` visibility gate, the `readAt IS NULL` unread filter, unread count computation, and edge cases — all notifications dismissed, all read, empty list, mixed state.
- Mark-as-read mutation logic: verify `readAt` is set to a timestamp, that `dismissedAt` is untouched, and that a record belonging to a different user is rejected.
- Dismiss mutation logic: verify `dismissedAt` is set, and that cross-user records are rejected.
- Bulk variants of the above: verify scoping to `userId` only.

**Integration tests (Vitest + real PostgreSQL test instance — no mocks):**
- `GET /api/notifications` — returns only `dismissedAt IS NULL` records for the requesting user, ordered `createdAt DESC`, max 50; does not return other users' notifications.
- `PATCH /api/notifications/[id]/read` — sets `readAt`; returns 404 when notification belongs to another user.
- `PATCH /api/notifications/read-all` — bulk sets `readAt` for all unread, non-dismissed records of the requesting user only; does not affect other users.
- `PATCH /api/notifications/[id]/dismiss` — sets `dismissedAt`; returns 404 on wrong-user access.
- `PATCH /api/notifications/dismiss-all` — bulk sets `dismissedAt` for all non-dismissed records of the requesting user only.

**Component tests (React Testing Library):**
- Notification panel renders unread badge with correct count.
- Unread notification has the correct ARIA/visual class; read notification does not.
- Clicking "Mark as read" on an item triggers the correct mutation and transitions the item's visual state.
- Clicking "Mark all as read" triggers the bulk mutation and clears the unread visual treatment from all items.
- Clicking dismiss removes the item from the rendered list.
- Clicking "Dismiss all" clears the list and renders the empty-state component.
- Badge count is not rendered when unread count is zero.

**End-to-end tests (Playwright):**
- Full flow: user logs in → notification badge shows correct unread count → opens panel → sees unread items highlighted → clicks "Mark all as read" → badge drops to zero → clicks "Dismiss all" → empty state is displayed.
- Navigation flow: user clicks a notification with a `resourceType`/`resourceId` → is routed to the correct resource page → notification is marked read on return to panel.

**Acceptance criteria:** The feature is not considered shippable until all integration tests pass against a real PostgreSQL instance and the Playwright e2e suite completes without flakiness across three consecutive runs.

---

## 6. Out of Scope

- **Real-time push delivery (WebSockets / SSE):** The panel fetches on open only. Live push without page interaction is a meaningful infrastructure investment deferred to a follow-on iteration.
- **Email or mobile push digests:** Notification delivery channels outside the in-app center are a separate product concern with their own opt-in/preferences surface.
- **Notification preferences and muting:** Per-user controls over which notification types they receive, and at what frequency, are deferred to a dedicated settings feature.
- **Notification creation / event wiring:** Which application events generate notifications for which users is explicitly out of scope. This PRD defines the data model and write contract, but the integration of specific event sources is owned by each feature team.
- **Pagination beyond the initial 50 records:** Infinite scroll and "load more" are deferred; the 50-record limit is sufficient for v1 and avoids scope creep on the panel UX.
- **Filtering and search within the panel:** Filtering by notification type, date range, or keyword search is deferred.
- **Notification grouping or threading:** Collapsing multiple related notifications into a single group (e.g., "3 comments on Task X") is a v2 concern.
- **Admin broadcast notifications:** Organization-wide or role-targeted admin-created notifications are a separate administrative feature.
- **Read receipts visible to other users:** Whether a notification was read is private to the recipient; no social visibility of read state is included.

---

## 7. Further Notes

- **`NotificationType` enum longevity:** The initial set of types (`task_assigned`, `comment_added`, `mention`, `status_changed`) should be treated as a starting vocabulary, not a closed list. Enum extension in PostgreSQL requires a migration; consider whether a `text` column with application-layer validation better serves the team's migration velocity.
- **Index strategy:** As the `Notification` table grows, query performance on the listing endpoint depends on the index on `(userId, dismissedAt, createdAt DESC)`. This should be added in the same migration that creates the table.
- **Write-side contract documentation:** A follow-on internal tech note should document the notification service write interface so feature teams can integrate event wiring without reading this PRD. The interface itself (event type + userId + optional resource pointer) is intentionally thin.
- **Retention policy:** Dismissed notifications accumulate indefinitely in the current design. A future housekeeping job to purge dismissed records older than N days (e.g., 90) should be planned before the table becomes a storage concern at scale.
- **Accessibility:** The badge count must have an accessible label (e.g., `aria-label="12 unread notifications"`). The panel must be keyboard-navigable and trap focus when open, per WCAG 2.1 AA. These are acceptance criteria, not enhancements.
- **Related features:** This PRD pairs naturally with a future "Notification Preferences" settings page and with per-feature event-wiring PRDs (e.g., "Task Assignment Notifications", "Comment Mention Notifications") that will use the write contract defined here.

# PRD: Notes Full-Text Search

**Author:** Relay Studio Agent
**Date:** 2026-05-09

---

## 1. Problem Statement

As teams accumulate notes over time, finding a specific piece of information becomes increasingly painful. Today, users must manually browse or scroll through their notes list, relying on memory for rough location or date. There is no way to search by content — only by browsing. When a user vaguely remembers that "someone wrote something about the Q3 roadmap," they have no efficient path to that note. This wastes time, erodes trust in the notes feature as a reliable knowledge store, and pushes users toward external tools that do offer search. For power users with hundreds of notes, the experience is effectively broken.

---

## 2. Solution

Users gain a search bar that instantly searches across all their notes — both titles and content — as they type. Results appear in a panel showing which notes matched, accompanied by a short contextual excerpt (snippet) from the note body with the matching search terms visually highlighted. Results are ranked by relevance so the most pertinent notes surface first. Clicking any result navigates directly to that note. The experience feels fast and responsive: no page reloads, no waiting — just type and see.

---

## 3. User Stories

- **US-001:** As a team member, I want to search my notes by keyword, so that I can find a specific note without having to browse through the entire list.
- **US-002:** As a team member, I want to see a short excerpt from each matching note alongside the result, so that I can confirm it's the note I'm looking for before opening it.
- **US-003:** As a team member, I want the matched search terms highlighted in the snippet, so that I can immediately see why a result was returned.
- **US-004:** As a team member, I want search results ordered by relevance, so that the most closely matching notes appear at the top.
- **US-005:** As a team member, I want to see a result count alongside my results, so that I know how many notes matched my query.
- **US-006:** As a team member, I want to see a clear "no results" message when nothing matches, so that I know the search ran successfully and my query simply didn't match any notes.
- **US-007:** As a team member, I want results to update as I type (with debouncing), so that I don't have to press Enter or click a button to trigger a search.
- **US-008:** As a team member, I want to click a search result and be taken directly to that note, so that I can move seamlessly from finding to reading.

---

## 4. Implementation Decisions

### 4.1 Data Contract

**Model: `Note` (extended)**

The existing `Note` model is extended with a single new column to support full-text search. No new top-level entities are introduced.

| Field | Type | Nullability | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `searchVector` | `tsvector` | nullable | computed | Maintained by a database trigger; concatenation of `title` and `content` weighted A and B respectively |

**Lifecycle / Visibility:**
- The `searchVector` column is updated on every `INSERT` and `UPDATE` to a `Note` row via a PostgreSQL trigger. It is never written by application code directly.
- Search queries gate on the same visibility conditions as the existing note list (e.g., non-deleted notes belonging to the authenticated user's team/workspace). No separate visibility flag is introduced for search.
- Soft-deleted notes (if the project uses a `deletedAt` timestamp pattern) are excluded from search results using the same `WHERE deletedAt IS NULL` gate already applied to note queries.

**Index:**
- A GIN index is added on `Note.searchVector` to support efficient full-text lookups at scale.

**Search Result shape (API response, not a persisted entity):**

| Field | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | `string` | Note ID |
| `title` | `string` | Note title |
| `snippet` | `string` | HTML string with `<mark>` tags wrapping matched terms, generated by `ts_headline` |
| `rank` | `number` | Floating-point relevance score from `ts_rank` |
| `createdAt` | `string (ISO 8601)` | For display in results |
| `updatedAt` | `string (ISO 8601)` | For display in results |

**Relationships:** No new relationships. The search feature reads from the existing `Note → User/Team` relationship.

---

### 4.2 Tracer Bullet Slices

> **Slice 1 — Bare keyword search returns matching note titles**
> *Behavior:* A user types a query into a new search input; the server queries the `searchVector` GIN index and returns a list of matching note titles with their IDs, which the UI renders as a simple list.
> *Cuts through:* `Note.searchVector` column + GIN index migration, `ts_query` search logic in the notes data layer, new `GET /api/notes/search?q=` endpoint (authenticated, scoped to user's workspace), minimal search input component + results list rendering titles only.

> **Slice 2 — Snippets with highlighted terms appear in results**
> *Behavior:* Each result in the list now includes a short excerpt from the note body with matched terms wrapped in `<mark>` tags, giving the user immediate context about why the note matched.
> *Cuts through:* `ts_headline()` call added to the search query producing an HTML snippet, `snippet` field added to the API response shape, result list item component renders the snippet as sanitized HTML with highlighted marks styled via CSS.

> **Slice 3 — Results ranked by relevance with count displayed**
> *Behavior:* The results are ordered so the most relevant notes appear first, and the UI shows "X results for [query]" above the list.
> *Cuts through:* `ts_rank()` score computed and used in `ORDER BY` in the search query, total count included in API response envelope, result count banner rendered above the list.

> **Slice 4 — Empty state for zero-result queries**
> *Behavior:* When a query matches no notes, the user sees a clear empty-state message ("No notes found for '[query]'") rather than a blank or broken panel.
> *Cuts through:* API returns `{ results: [], total: 0 }` cleanly (no 404), UI conditionally renders an empty-state component when `total === 0`.

> **Slice 5 — Debounced live search with loading state**
> *Behavior:* As the user types, results update automatically after a short pause (300 ms debounce), and a loading indicator is shown during the in-flight request so the user knows the search is running.
> *Cuts through:* Debounce hook wired to the search input's `onChange`, loading state managed in the search component, loading indicator rendered in the results panel during pending requests.

> *Behavior:* The user clicks any result in the list and is navigated directly to that note's detail view, with the note fully rendered.

### 4.3 Other Implementation Decisions

**Search query building:**
- Raw user input must be sanitized and converted to a `tsquery` using `plainto_tsquery('english', ?)` rather than `to_tsquery`, so arbitrary user input (including punctuation and unbalanced operators) does not cause query parse errors. Stemming is handled by the `english` dictionary.

**Snippet configuration:**
- `ts_headline` is configured with a short max word count (≈30 words), `StartSel='<mark>'`, `StopSel='</mark>'`, and `HighlightAll=false` (show only the most relevant fragment, not the full content). These options are centralized in the search data-layer module so they can be tuned without touching the API handler.

**Snippet HTML safety:**
- The snippet field is server-generated and contains only `<mark>` tags injected by `ts_headline`. The UI component must strip all other HTML tags before rendering (or use a tight allowlist sanitizer) to prevent any stored XSS via note content.

**Minimum query length:**
- Queries shorter than 2 characters return an empty result set immediately (client-side gate) without hitting the server, to avoid expensive single-character wildcard scans.

**Pagination:**
- The search endpoint accepts `limit` (default 20, max 50) and `offset` parameters. The UI for this slice shows a single page of results; infinite scroll or pagination controls are deferred (see §6).

**Trigger maintenance:**
- The `searchVector` column is kept current via a PostgreSQL trigger (`BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE`) rather than application-level code, so bulk imports, migrations, and direct DB writes all keep the index consistent without requiring application involvement.

**Scope isolation:**
- The search query must always include a `WHERE userId = ? OR teamId = ?` (or equivalent workspace scoping) gate consistent with how the existing note list endpoint scopes results. The search module must not expose cross-workspace results under any input.

**Performance constraint:**
- Search queries should return within 200 ms at p95 for workspaces with up to 10,000 notes. The GIN index is the primary mechanism; if query plans degrade, `ts_rank_cd` (cover density ranking) is a drop-in alternative with better performance on large corpora.

**Error handling:**
- If `plainto_tsquery` still fails (edge case: some locales), the search endpoint returns a structured `400` with a user-facing message ("Search query is invalid — please try different terms"). Network failures surface as a non-blocking error banner in the search panel; the input remains active.

## 5. Testing Decisions

**Philosophy:** Tests cover observable behavior (what the API returns, what the UI renders) — not internal query construction or implementation details.

**Unit tests (Vitest):**
- The snippet-sanitizer utility is unit-tested covering: input with no HTML tags, input with only `<mark>` tags (passthrough), input with mixed foreign HTML tags (strip all but `<mark>`), empty string input, and null/undefined input.
- The query minimum-length gate is tested for queries of length 0, 1, and 2 characters.

**Integration tests (Vitest + a test PostgreSQL database, following existing patterns in the project):**
- The search data-layer module is integration-tested against a real PostgreSQL instance with seeded `Note` rows. Scenarios: exact keyword match on title, exact keyword match on content, partial stem match (e.g., "run" matches "running"), multi-word query, query with no matches (returns empty), query with special characters that would break `to_tsquery` (handled safely by `plainto_tsquery`), soft-deleted notes excluded from results, notes from a different workspace excluded from results.

**API/Route tests (Vitest + supertest or equivalent, following existing Next.js API route test patterns):**
- `GET /api/notes/search` tested for: unauthenticated request returns 401, query below min length returns empty results without DB call, valid query returns expected response shape (`results`, `total` fields present), `limit` and `offset` params respected.

**E2E tests (Playwright, following existing e2e patterns in the project):**
- A single happy-path E2E test: log in, type a known keyword into the search input, assert at least one result appears with the keyword highlighted in the snippet, click the result, assert the note detail page loads.
- An empty-state E2E test: type a query that matches no notes, assert the empty-state message is visible.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- All unit and integration tests pass in CI.
- E2E happy-path and empty-state tests pass in CI.
- Manual smoke test: search for a term present in 5+ notes, confirm results are ranked (most relevant first), snippets are legible, and clicking a result opens the correct note.

---

## 6. Out of Scope

- **Pagination / infinite scroll for results** — The initial slice returns up to 20 results. Paginating through large result sets is deferred; most queries will surface the relevant note in the top results.
- **Filtering by date range, author, or tag** — Faceted search is a natural next step but adds significant UI complexity. Deferred to a follow-on feature.
- **Search over attachments or embedded files** — Only note title and content (text) are indexed. PDF/image OCR is a separate, much larger effort.
- **Saved searches / search history** — No persistence of past queries. Deferred.
- **Boolean query syntax (AND/OR/NOT) exposed to users** — `plainto_tsquery` handles natural language; explicit boolean operators in the search box are not supported. A power-user query mode is deferred.
- **Search analytics / query logging** — Instrumenting what users search for (for product insights) is deferred to avoid scope creep and privacy considerations.
- **Cross-workspace/global admin search** — Search is scoped strictly to the authenticated user's workspace. Admin-level cross-workspace search is out of scope.
- **Fuzzy / typo-tolerant matching** — PostgreSQL FTS does stemming but not fuzzy matching (e.g., "meting" will not find "meeting"). Trigram-based fuzzy search via `pg_trgm` is a potential follow-on.
- **Real-time index updates for collaborative notes** — If notes are edited simultaneously by multiple users, the `searchVector` trigger fires per save, not per keystroke. Mid-edit content is not indexed until the note is saved.

---

## 7. Further Notes

- **PostgreSQL FTS is the right default here.** The project already uses PostgreSQL, and native FTS with `tsvector`/`tsquery` + GIN index delivers production-grade search for teams up to tens of thousands of notes without introducing a new infrastructure dependency (Elasticsearch, Typesense, etc.). If usage patterns outgrow PostgreSQL FTS, the search data-layer module's isolation means the backend can be swapped without touching the API or UI.
- **Prisma compatibility:** If the project uses Prisma as its ORM, the `searchVector` column should be declared as `Unsupported("tsvector")` in the Prisma schema and the trigger created via a raw migration. The search query itself will be a `$queryRaw` call. This is the standard Prisma pattern for PostgreSQL FTS.
- **Accessibility:** The search input and results list must meet WCAG 2.1 AA: the input has a visible label, results are keyboard-navigable (arrow keys + Enter), and `<mark>` elements are announced by screen readers (they are by default in most browsers).
- **Open question:** Should search scope default to "my notes only" or "all notes in the workspace visible to me"? The PRD assumes workspace-scoped (all notes the user has access to). This should be confirmed with stakeholders before implementation begins.
- **Related work:** This feature is a prerequisite for any future "smart suggestions" or AI-assisted recall feature, which would need a fast search layer as its retrieval backbone.

# PRD: Multi-Tenant Seat-Based Billing

**Author:** Relay Studio Agent
**Date:** 2026-05-09

---

## 1. Problem Statement

Organizations using the platform today have no unified way to manage billing across their entire team. Each user is billed independently, forcing finance and operations teams to reconcile dozens of separate invoices instead of a single consolidated account. There is no concept of seats — so when a new employee joins, billing is ad hoc and invisible to the admin who owns the budget.

When an organization needs to upgrade or downgrade their plan mid-cycle, the current system has no proration logic. Admins either lose money (paying for a full period after downgrading) or feel overcharged (paying full price for the upgraded plan on day one). Neither outcome builds trust.

Most critically, when a payment fails today, nothing happens automatically. Accounts fall silently into delinquency. Team members lose access without warning, admins are not notified with enough time to act, and there is no automated recovery path. This causes service interruptions, frustrated users, and avoidable churn that could be prevented by a structured retry and communication workflow.

---

## 2. Solution

Organizations get a single, unified billing account. An admin can subscribe their organization to a seat-based plan, choosing the number of seats they need upfront. As their team grows or shrinks, they can add or remove seats at any time. Billing is always consolidated into one invoice per organization per period — no more fragmented per-user charges.

When an admin changes their plan mid-cycle — whether upgrading to unlock more features or downgrading to reduce cost — the platform automatically calculates a prorated charge or credit for the remaining days in the billing period. The upcoming invoice shows a clear, itemized breakdown so there are never any surprise amounts.

When a payment fails, the platform immediately notifies the admin by email and shows a persistent in-app banner. It then retries the charge automatically on a published schedule, giving the team a grace period to resolve the issue. Admins can update their payment method at any point during the retry window to trigger an immediate re-attempt. If all retries are exhausted, the account is suspended — but only after clear, escalating communications. Reinstatement is immediate upon successful payment.
